response.title: A Smarter Way to Water the Garden
response.passage:
When the school garden club prepared its spring planting day, it expected twenty volunteers. The city had advised residents to limit outdoor water use after weeks without rain. To divide the work, the students agreed to cooperate instead of letting each team water at random. One group measured the soil, while another checked how much water each bed needed.

At first, the club believed the two rain barrels would be enough. By Friday, however, the barrels held only a quarter of the water the planting plan required, so the club faced a serious shortage. The students then asked the cafeteria to save clean rinse water from washing vegetables. They placed a marked bucket beside the sink and explained that only vegetable-rinse water should go into it. During lunch, one student agreed to observe the bucket and record the amount every fifteen minutes.

The first day's notes showed that the bucket filled twice as fast as expected. That extra supply allowed the club to water the seedlings without opening the outdoor tap. Even so, they chose to reserve one full bucket for emergencies instead of using every drop that afternoon. When the next dry week arrived, the saved water kept the youngest plants alive, and the club shared its collection method with another school.
